fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Verse 12 says they bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. I think this is a heavy part of the story. Their oath is tied to eating and drinking.
Close, but work and travel aren't in the oath. Verse 12 says they bound themselves not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. Only eating and drinking are named in it.
That's it, baker. Verse 13 says more than forty of them were involved in this plot. More than forty means the number was bigger than forty. That's a whole lot of men for one plan.

Ninety isn't the number the text gives. Verse 13 says more than forty of them were involved in the plot. The text doesn't give a count beyond that, so I can't tell you ninety. Forty is the number in the verse.

Right on target. In verses 14 and 15 the plotters go to the chief priests and elders and tell them to have the Sanhedrin petition the commander to bring Paul down. The Sanhedrin is the Jewish council. The whole plan hangs on that one request.

The governor isn't part of their request. In verses 14 and 15 they go to the chief priests and elders and ask for a petition to the commander to bring Paul down. The governor, Felix, shows up later in the story, and that's the commander's doing. The plotters only want Paul brought down to them.
Yes, friend. Verse 15 says the request is to be made on the pretext of examining his case more carefully. A pretext is a cover story. Right after that they say, “We are ready to kill him on the way.”
Right. Paul doesn't go himself. He calls one of the centurions in verse 17 and asks him to take the young man to the commander. The nephew carries the news in.
Yes, baker. In verse 20 the nephew tells the commander the Jews will ask him to bring Paul to the Sanhedrin tomorrow. The commander hears about it from the nephew. That's a head start.
That's right. In verse 22 the commander instructs the young man, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported this to me.” The text doesn't give his reason. It only gives the instruction.
That's the spot. In verse 23 the commander says to go to Caesarea. Verse 24 says to take Paul safely to Governor Felix, and in verse 33 the horsemen deliver him to the governor in Caesarea.
Damascus isn't the place the commander names. Verse 23 says the escort goes to Caesarea. Damascus isn't mentioned in this passage at all.
Not in daylight, friend. Verse 23 has the commander say to go in the third hour of the night. That's a night departure, not a daytime one.

That's it, baker. Verse 29 has Lysias write that the accusation involved questions about their own law. He also writes that he found no charge worthy of death or imprisonment. That's what he tells Felix in the letter.

That's right. Verse 32 says that the next day the soldiers returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with Paul. Verse 33 says the horsemen arrived in Caesarea and presented Paul to the governor.
The spearmen aren't the ones named. Verse 32 says the soldiers returned to the barracks and let the horsemen go on with Paul. The text names the horsemen as the ones who go on with him.

That's the one, baker. Felix reads the whole letter and then asks one plain question: what province is Paul from? Short question, short answer: Cilicia (v34). Then he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.”

Galatia isn't what Felix hears. He reads the letter, asks what province Paul is from, and learns it's Cilicia (v34). Then he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Felix gets one answer, and it isn't Galatia.

Macedonia isn't the province here. Verse 34 says Felix asks what province Paul is from, and Cilicia is what he learns. Then he says, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Macedonia gets no mention in this passage.
